conversation.content:
Hi there, I’m Dr. Morales, a perinatal mental-health specialist. I’m here to make sure you’re getting the support you deserve after having your baby. Today we’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS—to check in on how you’ve been feeling over the past week. It’s just 10 short questions; there are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays between us unless you give me permission to involve someone else. My goal is simply to understand how things are going so we can figure out the best next steps together.

Ready to start?  
First question: In the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?
Oh—yeah, I’ve still been laughing. Like, yesterday my husband made that goofy face while he was changing the diaper, and I couldn’t help but crack up. So… most of the time, I guess.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most of the time.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Most of the time. I still get excited about little outings—like our morning stroller walks or the coffee run on Fridays. There are moments when I’m too tired to feel super enthusiastic, but generally I still find myself looking forward to things.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not very often. I mean, if the baby spits up right after I’ve changed her outfit, I might think, “Should I have burped her longer?” but I don’t really dwell on it. I figure babies are just messy and unpredictable, so I don’t stay stuck on blaming myself.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Hardly ever. I’ll get a little flutter of worry if her breathing sounds funny or if she sleeps longer than usual, but it passes once I check on her. It’s not like I’m walking around feeling anxious all day for no reason.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not at all. I haven’t had any of those out-of-nowhere scared or panicky moments.
Things have been getting on top of me
Only occasionally. Some afternoons when she won’t nap and the laundry’s piled up I feel a bit swamped, but it’s not a constant thing—mostly I manage to muddle through.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
Never. Once I finally lie down, I’m out pretty quickly—exhaustion helps, I guess. I haven’t felt so upset that it kept me awake.
I have felt sad or miserable
Not very often. Maybe once or twice this week I felt a little weepy when I was overtired, but it didn’t stick around.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Hardly ever. I think I teared up one evening when the baby wouldn’t settle and I was really tired, but it was just for a minute—no full-on crying spells.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
Never. That hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

You shared that you're generally enjoying your new baby-still laughing at your husband's silly faces, looking forward to coffee runs, and managing the day-to-day with only the occasional overwhelmed afternoon. Moments of tiredness or brief worries pop up, but they pass quickly and don't cloud your overall mood.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 7, Risk Level: Depression not likely
**Reasoning:** EPDS items show preserved enjoyment (<quote>most of the time</quote>), minimal anxiety (<quote>hardly ever</quote>), and no self-harm thoughts. Total score of 7 falls below the 8-point threshold for likely <med>postpartum depression</med>. Symptoms do not meet <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> (insufficient duration/severity of low mood, anhedonia, or neuro-vegetative signs). This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Keep routine well-baby and postpartum visits; re-screen with EPDS at 6-week check
2. Continue prioritising rest-nap when baby naps and accept help with chores
3. Maintain social contacts like your stroller walks for mood support
4. Return sooner if low mood, persistent anxiety, or self-harm thoughts emerge
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 7: Postpartum Depression Screening – EPDS Responses (10 items)

Symptom profile  
– Mood: transient sadness/crying only when overtired; no persistent low mood  
– Enjoyment: maintained (“most of the time”)  
– Anxiety: situational, brief, no panic episodes  
– Guilt/self-blame: minimal and situation-specific  
– Coping: occasional afternoon “swamped” feeling; overall managing  
– Sleep: good once settled; no mood-related insomnia  
– Safety: denies self-harm thoughts

Pattern  
Predominantly normative postpartum adjustment; no clustering of core depressive or anxiety symptoms; no safety concerns.

Screening significance  
Current responses do not indicate elevated risk for postpartum depression or anxiety. Continue routine perinatal support and re-screen at next visit or sooner if clinical picture changes.
